20	## What matters first
21	
22	The order of importance across the whole piece, outside charts and controls.
23	
24	- [ ] **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** → `references/layout.md` "One element dominates"; `references/art-direction.md` "One focal point"; `references/art-direction.md` "Emphasis through contrast, not volume" _(off-list source)_; `references/layout.md` "Contrast of scale gives the page tension"; `references/art-direction.md` "Dominant scale contrast" _(off-list source)_; `references/art-direction.md` "Variety to avoid monotony"
25	- [ ] **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** → `references/art-direction.md` "Visual hierarchy has distinct levels"; `references/typography.md` "Weak contrast is worse than none"; `references/typography.md` "Sizes come from a scale"
26	- [ ] **Where headings are clearly larger than the text, do they also differ from it in weight, form, or color?** → `references/typography.md` "Contrast from more than size"
27	
28	## Arrangement and space
29	
30	Where elements sit and the space between them, outside charts and controls.
31	
32	- [ ] **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** → `references/layout.md` "One grid governs the page"; `references/art-direction.md` "Use a grid"; `references/layout.md` "Pictures fit the grid"; `references/layout.md` "Equal intervals between columns"; `references/art-direction.md` "Repetition and rhythm are regular enough to read"
33	- [ ] **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** → `references/layout.md` "Break the grid decisively or not at all"; `references/art-direction.md` "Alignment: every element has a visible relationship"; `references/layout.md` "Optical alignment over mathematical alignment"
34	- [ ] **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** → `references/typography.md` "Lines of text align across columns"
35	- [ ] **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** → `references/layout.md` "Space shows the groups"; `references/art-direction.md` "Proximity groups related items"; `references/typography.md` "Headings sit with the text they introduce"; `references/dataviz.md` "Group related items by proximity, enclosure, and similarity"; `references/layout.md` "Unrelated elements do not crowd each other"
36	- [ ] **Does each card, panel, tint, or border hold exactly one group, with no group split across boxes?** → `references/basics.md` "Boxes do not split or join groups"
37	- [ ] **Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups or shapes formed between unrelated ones?** → `references/art-direction.md` "Gestalt grouping: similarity, continuity, closure"
38	- [ ] **Does each element stay clear of the others, with no text or box overlapping or touching another?** → (no catalog entry: judge as taste or common sense, and say so)
39	- [ ] **Do text and boxes keep a margin from the edge of the page or screen?** → `references/basics.md` "Content keeps clear of the page edge"
40	- [ ] **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** → `references/layout.md` "White space is gathered, not scattered"; `references/art-direction.md` "Negative space is deliberate"
41	- [ ] **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** → `references/layout.md` "Balance"; `references/art-direction.md` "Balance (symmetrical or asymmetrical)"
42	- [ ] **Is each centered or symmetric placement of blocks or of the main subject there for a reason the piece shows, rather than by habit?** → `references/layout.md` "No central axis by default"; `references/art-direction.md` "Symmetry is chosen, and static by default"; `references/art-direction.md` "Rule of thirds and off-center subject placement" _(off-list source)_
43	- [ ] **Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion, such as halves, thirds, or the golden section, rather than arbitrary splits?** → `references/art-direction.md` "Golden ratio and proportional division (use sparingly)"
44	- [ ] **Does the arrangement lead the eye from the first element through the rest, with no line, gaze, or pointing shape that leads it off the edge?** → `references/art-direction.md` "Clear eye path"; `references/art-direction.md` "Leading lines and directional movement" _(off-list source)_

46	## Text
47	
48	Setting and reading text, outside charts and controls.
49	
50	- [ ] **Is body text large enough to read, at least as large as the menu and button text around it (12 pt or more in print for low vision)?** → `references/basics.md` "Body text is not smaller than the menu and button text"; `references/accessibility.md` "Low-vision large-print guidance" _(off-list source)_
51	- [ ] **Are captions, labels, and legal text large enough to read (11 pt or more on iOS)?** → `references/basics.md` "Captions and labels are not too small to read"
52	- [ ] **Is paragraph text set upright in a plain face made for reading, not in italic, underline, script, blackletter, or a display face?** → `references/basics.md` "Paragraphs are not set in a decorative face"; `references/accessibility.md` "Dyslexia-friendly typography" _(off-list source)_
53	- [ ] **Do the typefaces follow one plan, one family or a few plainly different faces, with no face that nearly matches another and no extra unrelated face?** → `references/typography.md` "Typefaces in concord or in clear contrast, never in conflict"
54	- [ ] **Is small text set in a weight heavy enough to hold up, with hairline weights kept to large sizes?** → `references/typography.md` "Weight and stroke thickness at small sizes"
55	- [ ] **Does text on a plain background reach 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text), placeholder and helper text included?** → `references/basics.md` "Text does not read as faint"; `references/color.md` "Body text contrast (WCAG AA)"; `references/accessibility.md` "Text contrast (minimum)"; `references/color.md` "Placeholder, disabled and decorative text exemptions"
56	- [ ] **Does text over a photo, gradient, or texture stay readable at the worst point behind it?** → `references/layout.md` "Figure and ground are unambiguous"; `references/color.md` "Text over images and gradients"
57	- [ ] **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** → `references/typography.md` "Line length (measure)"
58	- [ ] **Does the space between lines of a paragraph suit its line length, neither cramped nor so loose that the lines drift apart?** → `references/typography.md` "Leading suits the measure"; `references/accessibility.md` "Dyslexia-friendly line length, spacing, and background" _(off-list source)_
59	- [ ] **Is a heading of two or more lines set tight enough to read as one unit?** → `references/typography.md` "Heading lines hold together"
60	- [ ] **Are paragraphs of several lines set flush left?** → `references/basics.md` "Paragraphs are not centered or right-aligned"
61	- [ ] **Does justified text keep even word spaces, with no holes or rivers of white?** → `references/typography.md` "Even word spacing in justified text"; `references/typography.md` "Rivers of white space"
62	- [ ] **Is the right edge of ragged text gently uneven, with no staircase, wedge, or regular long-short pattern?** → `references/typography.md` "Rag quality in ragged-right text"
63	- [ ] **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** → `references/typography.md` "Widows, orphans, and runts"
64	- [ ] **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** → `references/typography.md` "Line breaks in headings and short text"
65	- [ ] **Are paragraphs marked by an indent or by space, never both, with the first paragraph after a heading flush left?** → `references/typography.md` "Paragraph marks: indent or space, not both"
66	- [ ] **Does the left edge of each text block stay crisp, with wrapped list lines under the first word and opening quotation marks hung outside?** → `references/typography.md` "Hanging bullets and punctuation"
67	- [ ] **Is long text broken up by headings, short paragraphs, or lists?** → `references/basics.md` "Text is broken into chunks"
68	- [ ] **Is every sentence or paragraph set in mixed case, with capitals kept to short headings and labels?** → `references/basics.md` "Long text is not set in all capitals"
69	- [ ] **Does each emphasized phrase change one thing only (italic, bold, or small capitals)?** → `references/typography.md` "One change at a time for emphasis"
70	- [ ] **Are large headings set with tighter letter and word spacing than the text?** → `references/typography.md` "Display type is spaced tighter than text"
71	- [ ] **In large mixed-case type, do letter pairs look evenly spaced, with no gaps and no collisions?** → `references/typography.md` "Kerning"
72	- [ ] **Is lower-case text set with its typeface's own letter spacing, neither tracked out nor squeezed?** → `references/typography.md` "Letterspacing (tracking) of text"
73	- [ ] **Are strings of capitals and small capitals letterspaced?** → `references/typography.md` "Letterspace capitals and small caps"
74	- [ ] **In large type, are "fi" and "fl" joined as ligatures where the face's f reaches into the next letter?** → `references/typography.md` "Ligatures"

77	- [ ] **Do columns of numbers use tabular figures aligned on the decimal point or the right edge?** → `references/typography.md` "Figures in tables and text"

content.content:
=== references/accessibility.md
### Reflow

- **Rule:** At a 320 CSS px wide viewport (400% zoom of 1280 px) content reflows to one column with no horizontal scrolling and no loss of information. Exceptions: data tables, maps, diagrams, video, and toolbars needing two-dimensional layout; vertical content uses 256 CSS px height.
- **Source:** WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (AA)
- **Link:** https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/reflow.html
- **Caveat:** breaks NG-10 because it needs a render at 320 px wide, which one image cannot show.

=== references/basics.md
### Content keeps clear of the page edge

- **Rule:** Text and boxes sit inside the type area, with a margin between them and the edge of the page.
- **Look for:** Does any text, button, or form field sit right against an edge of the page, with almost no space between it and the edge?
- **Source:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design* (1981), sections "Margin proportions" and "Construction of the type area".

=== references/layout.md
### One element dominates

- **Rule:** The order of importance is plain: one element is seen first and the rest follow. Tschichold asks that logical order be shown by differences of size, and Hofmann builds compositions from contrasts such as much against little.
- **Look for:** Are there three or more elements of the same size and weight competing to be seen first, with none clearly stronger than the others?
- **Source:** Tschichold, *The New Typography* (1928), chapter "The principles of the new typography"; Hofmann, *Graphic Design Manual* (1965), the text chapters "The line" and "Confrontation".
- **Link:** https://www.neugraphic.com/tschichold/tschichold-text5.html
- **Fix (approved), Three or more elements compete to be seen first:** Make one element clearly the first thing seen and set the rest back by differences of size, so that the order of importance is plain (Tschichold, *The New Typography*).
- **How bad it gets:** not measured. Three or more elements given the same size, weight, and strength of color, with none clearly stronger than the others.

=== references/typography.md
### Sizes come from a scale

- **Rule:** Text sizes come from a small, deliberate scale, so that each size reads as its own level. Many sizes that are almost the same show that sizes were picked one at a time.
- **Look for:** Are there two blocks of ordinary paragraph text, in the same typeface and weight and with no heading role, where the letters of one block are a little larger than the letters of the other, so that the two blocks do not match when seen side by side or one after the other?
- **Source:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, section 3.1.1 "Don't compose without a scale", p. 45 (from the scan's OCR text): "limit yourself, at first, to a modest set of distinct and related intervals."

=== references/typography.md
### Contrast from more than size

- **Rule:** Average work builds every level of the hierarchy from size alone, so headings grow very large while their weight, form, and color stay the same as the text. Considered work pairs a smaller step in size with a change of weight, of form (capitals, italic), of structure (serif against sans serif), or of color.
- **Look for:** Are the headings set in the same weight, style, and color as the body text, so that they differ from it only in size?
- **Source:** Dair, *Design with Type*, chapters 8a to 8g and chapter 9 "Multiplying the contrasts".
- **Fix (approved), Headings differ from the body text only in size:** Pair a smaller step in heading size with a change of weight, of form such as capitals or italic, of structure such as serif against sans serif, or of color (Dair, Design with Type, chapters 8a to 8g and 9).
- **How bad it gets:** not measured. Headings in the same face, weight, style, and color as the text, larger than it by a clear step.

=== references/ux.md
### Primary versus secondary action

- **Rule:** One primary action per view is visually dominant (filled, high contrast); secondary actions are lower emphasis (outline or text); cancel and tertiary actions are weakest. Two equal-weight filled buttons is a fault.
- **Source:** Material Design 3, "Buttons" guidance (emphasis levels); Apple HIG, "Buttons"; NN/g, "Visual Hierarchy" and "Button Design" guidance.
- **Link:** https://m3.material.io/components/buttons/guidelines

=== references/ux.md
### Redundancy and duplicate controls

- **Rule:** The same action is not offered twice on one screen without reason (two "Sign up" buttons beside each other, repeated links in the same block, header and footer copies competing). Duplicates dilute the primary action.
- **Look for:** Are there two buttons or links next to each other that do the same thing, with labels that mean the same action?
- **Source:** Nielsen heuristic 8 (aesthetic and minimalist design); Krug, *Don't Make Me Think* (2000), "get rid of half the words, then half of what's left."
- **Fix (approved), Two controls side by side do the same thing:** Keep one control for the action and remove its twin, or give the second control a different job, such as Cancel or See pricing.
- **How bad it gets:** not measured. One extra control sits next to the original, styled like the second control on the clean side, with a label that is a plain synonym ("Get started" and "Start now", "Save" and "Save changes"). The clean side shows a control with a different action in the same place.

=== references/layout.md
### White space is gathered, not scattered

- **Rule:** Ruder holds that the printed and the unprinted areas must stand in tension, and that the tension comes from contrast. Considered work gathers empty space into a few large, shaped areas set against dense ones. Average work spreads the same small gap between everything, so no space does any work, and it runs content up to the edges of the page.
- **Look for:** Does the page look evenly filled, with its empty space spread thin between everything and no open area large enough to give the eye a place to rest?
- **Source:** Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design* (1967), chapters "Contrasts" and "Form and counter-form"; Kunz, *Typography: Macro- and Microaesthetics* (1998), part two, on space and on form and counterform.

=== references/layout.md
### Balance

- **Rule:** Visual weight comes from size, darkness, color, and isolation, and where an element sits changes its weight. A layout may be symmetrical or not, but a heavy side needs a counterweight.
- **Look for:** Does one side of the page carry much more visual weight than the other, with nothing on the lighter side strong enough to balance it?
- **Source:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, chapter I "Balance", sections "Weight" and "Psychological and physical balance".

=== references/typography.md
### Line length (measure)

- **Rule:** A single column of paragraph text must not run so wide that the eye loses its place on the way back to the start of the next line. Bringhurst gives 45 to 75 characters as the comfortable range, 66 as the ideal, and 40 to 50 for text set in several columns.
- **Look for:** Does a paragraph of body text stretch in one column from the left margin of the page to the right margin, with no sidebar, image, or second column beside it, so that its lines are as wide as the page's content area?
- **Source:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style* (Version 3.0, 2004), section 2.1.2 "Choose a comfortable measure", p. 26 (from the scan's OCR text): "Anything from 45 to 75 characters is widely regarded as a satisfactory length of line for a single-column page".

=== references/typography.md
### Line breaks in headings and short text

- **Rule:** Headings, buttons, and captions break at natural phrase boundaries and do not split a word, a number and its unit, or a name across lines.
- **Source:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, section 2.4 "Etiquette of hyphenation and pagination", section 2.4.6 (link short numerical expressions with hard spaces), which supports a number and its unit; Hochuli, *Detail in Typography* (2008). UNVERIFIED: breaks in headings were not found in Bringhurst or in Hochuli.
- **Caveat:** it reads the words to judge where a line breaks, which is the content.

=== references/typography.md
### Widows, orphans, and runts

- **Rule:** A paragraph does not end with one short word alone on its last line, and a column does not begin with the last line of a paragraph. A heading does not sit at the foot of a column with its text in the next one.
- **Source:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, sections 2.4.2 (no short last-line word) and 2.4.8 (never begin a page with the last line of a paragraph). Both are supported. UNVERIFIED: a heading at the foot of a column was not found in Bringhurst.

=== references/typography.md
### Rag quality in ragged-right text

- **Rule:** The right edge of ragged text is gently uneven. It does not form a staircase, a wedge, or a regular long-short pattern.
- **Look for:** Trace the right ends of the lines of a left-aligned paragraph. Do they form a regular shape, either a straight diagonal slope where each line is shorter or longer than the one above, or a regular zigzag of long, short, long, short?

### Text contrast (minimum)

- **Rule:** Body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background; large text (at least 24 CSS px, or 18.66 CSS px bold) needs at least 3:1. Logos and disabled controls are exempt.

**First read.** The eye lands first on the dark intro paragraph, not the headline. The headline above it is a pale gray line only a touch larger, so it reads like a caption. Next comes the filled green "See boats and dates" button, then the white form on the right with its outlined "Search" button. It reads as a quiet, plain booking page for a canal boatyard. It feels calm but empty: no boat, no water, no price, and a lot of bare background. On the phone the page breaks: the two columns never stack, the nav wraps into a column beside the logo, the intro runs two or three words per line, and the form is pushed off the right edge of the screen.

**What it's for.** The home page of a narrowboat hire site, where people book a boat directly with the boatyard (as told to me).

**Verdict.** On desktop and tablet it works as a plain search page, but nothing on it leads, and it hides its one real selling point. On a phone it fails outright, because most of the booking form sits off the screen. Fix the phone layout first.

**What would move it most**
1. **The phone layout does not reflow, so the booking form is mostly off the screen.** The page is 587 px wide in a 390 px viewport (facts file, phone `notes`: "scrolls sideways"). The form starts at x 270 (`form.search` labels) and the Search button runs to x 564, so a phone visitor sees only a sliver of the form and must scroll sideways to book. The hero text is squeezed into a 119 px column: the intro runs 18 lines at 9 characters per line (`p.lead`, `characters_per_line` 9.1), the headline breaks into five lines, and "See boats and dates" wraps to two lines. The nav stacks into five lines beside the logo, and "Your booking" splits across two. This is a defect: the phone is where many people browse holidays, and here they cannot see the thing they came to use (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow). Direction: below tablet width, stack everything into one column, with headline, intro, form, then routes. Give the nav a phone treatment that fits on one row or folds away. Viewports: phone
2. **Nothing leads, because the headline is styled as the weakest text in the hero.** The h1 is 22 px, weight 400, in gray `#6b7574`. The lead under it is 20 px in near-black `#26302f`, and the nav is also 20 px (`font_size`, `h1`, `p.lead`, `nav.site-nav`). The darker paragraph wins, and the logo at 24 px competes too. That gives three sizes within 4 px of each other (24, 22, 20) and two more at 16 and 14: five sizes where three would do, and the top three read as one level (Bringhurst, 3.1.1). The h1 also differs from the body only by being lighter, which is the wrong direction for a heading (Dair, chapters 8 and 9). The visitor gets no clear first line to read, so the offer takes a second pass to find. This is a defect, plus a convention break. Direction: make the headline clearly the first thing seen, with a real step up in size and dark color, perhaps a heavier weight or the serif from the logo. Bring the nav down toward 16 px so it stops matching the lead (Tschichold, *The New Typography*). Viewports: all
3. **Two buttons do the same job, and the stronger style is on the weaker one.** "See boats and dates" (filled, `a.button`) and the form's "Search" (outlined, `button`) both lead to available boats. The form already holds the visitor's base, date, nights, and berths, so Search is the action that books. Yet the generic link gets the filled primary style, and the real action looks secondary. The visitor has to stop and work out which one to press, and whether the left button ignores what they set in the form. This is a defect (Material Design, emphasis levels; Nielsen heuristic 8 on duplicate controls). Direction: keep one action. Make the form's Search the filled primary, and remove the hero button or give it a different job. Viewports: all
4. **The copy buries the reason to book here, and the headline contradicts the routes.** "Hire a narrowboat for a week on the canal" could sit on any hire site. The real difference is the last sentence of the intro: "book it here with the boatyard that keeps it. No agency in the middle, and no fee on top of the hire." A visitor who skims stops before they reach it. "For a week" also clashes with the route list just below, which offers 4 nights and 10 nights. And "no fee on top of the hire" gives the visitor nothing to measure it against, because the page shows no hire price anywhere. The visitor cannot see the value for themselves; they must take it on trust. This is a defect. Direction: move the direct-booking point up into the headline or the line straight under it, and drop or loosen "for a week". Show the kind of fact that proves the claim, such as a from-price per week. That figure has to come from the boatyard. Viewports: all
5. **On wide screens the page splits to the edges and leaves a hole in the middle.** At 1920 px the text column stops at x 664 and the form starts at x 1517, so the eye has to cross about 850 px of nothing to get from the pitch to the form. At 1280 px there is a dead band of about 270 px under the hero button, above "Routes from Hartwell Junction". Nothing ties the two sides together, and the form looks like a sidebar instead of the point of the page. This is a defect for the eye path and balance (Arnheim, on balance; Ruder, on gathered space). Direction: put the layout in a max-width container so the text and the form sit as one group, and close the gap above the routes. Viewports: desktop, widescreen
6. **A holiday page with no picture of the holiday.** This is taste, but I would argue it hard. People hire a narrowboat for the boat and the water, and this page shows neither. The design is plain enough to carry a picture well. Direction: add a real photo of the boatyard's own boats or a stretch of a route, and avoid stock pictures. Viewports: all

**Smaller things.**
- The h1 and the gray route details ("7 nights, 38 locks") measure 4.46:1, just under 4.5:1 (`violations`). Darken the gray slightly; the h1 fix in item 2 covers the heading. Viewports: all
- The form field borders look pale gray on white, roughly 1.5:1 by eye (not measured), and on the start-date field the border is the only edge. Darken them to at least 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11). Viewports: all
- On the tablet the intro paragraph runs 24 characters per line (`p.lead`), far under 45, and ends with "hire." alone on the last line. Widen the text column or narrow the gap to the form. Viewports: tablet
- On the phone the route rows break a number from its unit ("12 / locks", "61 / locks"). Join each number and unit with a non-breaking space, or stack the details under the route name. Viewports: phone
- "Sat 14 June" looks like a free-text field, not a date picker. If it takes typed text, constrain it to a date input or picker (Nielsen heuristic 5). Viewports: all

**What's working.**
- The form is prefilled with sensible defaults (a base, a Saturday start, 7 nights, 4 people), so a visitor can press Search without typing. Keep that.
- The route list shows nights and locks for each route, which is exactly what a canal hirer weighs. "Routes from Hartwell Junction" follows the form's chosen base, which ties the two together.
- The palette is restrained, with one deep green, an off-white ground, and a serif wordmark. It suits a slow, unhurried holiday and looks like no template.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the route list updates when the Base field changes, and whether the route rows are meant to be links (they carry no link styling, and the facts file lists them as text, not targets).

**Checklist.**
The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (every element does a job)
What matters first: 3 lines, 0 yes, 3 no (one element dominates; distinct levels; contrast from more than size)
Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (margin from the edge; white space gathered; balance; eye path)
Text: 30 lines, 25 yes, 5 no (contrast; line length; rag; widows; line breaks)
Color: 9 lines, 9 yes
Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes (no pictures besides the logo)
Charts and data: skipped, no chart
Interface: 33 lines, 27 yes, 4 no (primary action; non-text contrast; valid inputs; reflow), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)
Template tells: 10 lines, 10 yes

1	**First read.** The eye lands first on the dark intro paragraph, not the headline. The headline above it is a pale gray line only a touch larger, so it reads like a caption. Next comes the filled green "See boats and dates" button, then the white form on the right with its outlined "Search" button. It reads as a quiet, plain booking page for a canal boatyard. It feels calm but empty: no boat, no water, no price, and a lot of bare background. On the phone the page breaks: the two columns never stack, the nav wraps into a column beside the logo, the intro runs two or three words per line, and the form is pushed off the right edge of the screen.
2	
3	**What it's for.** The home page of a narrowboat hire site, where people book a boat directly with the boatyard (as told to me).
4	
5	**Verdict.** On desktop and tablet it works as a plain search page, but nothing on it leads, and it hides its one real selling point. On a phone it fails outright, because most of the booking form sits off the screen. Fix the phone layout first.
6	
7	**What would move it most**
8	1. **The phone layout does not reflow, so the booking form is mostly off the screen.** The page is 587 px wide in a 390 px viewport (facts file, phone `notes`: "scrolls sideways"). The form starts at x 270 (`form.search` labels) and the Search button runs to x 564, so a phone visitor sees only a sliver of the form and must scroll sideways to book. The hero text is squeezed into a 119 px column: the intro runs 18 lines at 9 characters per line (`p.lead`, `characters_per_line` 9.1), the headline breaks into five lines, and "See boats and dates" wraps to two lines. The nav stacks into five lines beside the logo, and "Your booking" splits across two. This is a defect: the phone is where many people browse holidays, and here they cannot see the thing they came to use (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow). Direction: below tablet width, stack everything into one column, with headline, intro, form, then routes. Give the nav a phone treatment that fits on one row or folds away. Viewports: phone
9	2. **Nothing leads, because the headline is styled as the weakest text in the hero.** The h1 is 22 px, weight 400, in gray `#6b7574`. The lead under it is 20 px in near-black `#26302f`, and the nav is also 20 px (`font_size`, `h1`, `p.lead`, `nav.site-nav`). The darker paragraph wins, and the logo at 24 px competes too. That gives three sizes within 4 px of each other (24, 22, 20) and two more at 16 and 14: five sizes where three would do, and the top three read as one level (Bringhurst, 3.1.1). The h1 also differs from the body only by being lighter, which is the wrong direction for a heading (Dair, chapters 8 and 9). The visitor gets no clear first line to read, so the offer takes a second pass to find. This is a defect, plus a convention break. Direction: make the headline clearly the first thing seen, with a real step up in size and dark color, perhaps a heavier weight or the serif from the logo. Bring the nav down toward 16 px so it stops matching the lead (Tschichold, *The New Typography*). Viewports: all
10	3. **Two buttons do the same job, and the stronger style is on the weaker one.** "See boats and dates" (filled, `a.button`) and the form's "Search" (outlined, `button`) both lead to available boats. The form already holds the visitor's base, date, nights, and berths, so Search is the action that books. Yet the generic link gets the filled primary style, and the real action looks secondary. The visitor has to stop and work out which one to press, and whether the left button ignores what they set in the form. This is a defect (Material Design, emphasis levels; Nielsen heuristic 8 on duplicate controls). Direction: keep one action. Make the form's Search the filled primary, and remove the hero button or give it a different job. Viewports: all
11	4. **The copy buries the reason to book here, and the headline contradicts the routes.** "Hire a narrowboat for a week on the canal" could sit on any hire site. summary:
**Where it could go further.**
1. **Make the route list the core of the page.** The list under "Routes from Hartwell Junction" holds the only facts on the page that are about canal life: nights and locks for each route. Today it sits at the bottom like a footnote, set in small gray type. A stronger version would treat the routes as the main way into a holiday, not an extra under the form. The lock count would be the number that leads each row, because it tells a hirer if the trip is a hard one or a lazy one. That serves a direct booking site well: a boatyard knows its own water, and the route list is where it can show that, which no agency can. This is taste. No approved source makes this exact point, so I argue it on its own terms: the page should lead with the thing only this seller can show.
2. **Builds on finding 2. Let the Slowwater serif carry the whole voice of the page, not only the headline.** Today the serif is only in the wordmark, and the sans does everything else. A stronger version would use the serif for every line a visitor reads as a promise: the headline, the "Routes from…" heading, and the route names. The sans would stay for the working parts, such as labels, fields, and buttons. The name already promises a slow, unhurried trip. Give that promise one typeface and the booking tools another, and the page says "holiday" and "book" in two clear voices, so a visitor can see which part to read and which part to use. This is taste (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, on choosing a face that suits the text and pairing faces with clear roles).
3. **Builds on finding 3. Keep the deep green for the act of booking only.** After finding 3 the green moves to the form's Search button. The stronger step is to keep it off everything else, so that across the site the green always means "this books your boat." The palette is already restrained enough for one color to own one meaning. On a page that exists to take a direct booking, a color that always marks the booking step does the job that a second button would do badly. This is taste (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*, on keeping strong color for the primary action; Albers, *Interaction of Color*, on how one color reads differently in different settings).

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and no element the fix added or changed is a template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but an element the fix added or changed is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the fix added or changed as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. Added means the after image has it and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background. Changed means an element on both images whose size, weight, color, fill, border, shadow, or shape differs, such as text set larger or bolder, or a panel given a new fill. An added or changed element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and an element the fix added or changed is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.

summary:
**First read.** The eye lands first on the serif headline, "Hire a narrowboat direct from the boatyard that keeps it". It moves down to the intro, and then right to the filled teal Search button, which is now the only strong color on the page. The page reads as a calm, plain booking page for a small boatyard, with the offer and the form side by side as one group. It feels honest and quiet, but it has no picture, so it gives the viewer nothing to look forward to. On the tablet and the phone, the same order stacks into one column: headline, intro, link, form, routes. On the widescreen, the same 1024 px group sits centered.

**What it's for.** It gets a visitor to search for a narrowboat and book it direct from the boatyard (from the work order's crit).

**Verdict.** The fixes helped a lot. The phone layout now reflows, the headline leads, there is one primary action, and the text and the form sit together at every width. The biggest things still in the way are two facts that only the boatyard can supply: a price to back "no fee on top of the hire", and a real photo of the boats or the water.

**Finding status**
- phone-layout-no-reflow: closed. On the phone, page_width is 390 and p.lead has 35 characters per line. The nav fits on one row and the whole form is on screen in one column.
- headline-weakest-text: closed. The h1 is 40 px (32 px on the phone), set in the logo's serif, color #26302f with 12.75:1 contrast. The lead is 20 px, the logo is 24 px, and the nav is 16 px, at all four viewports.
- duplicate-primary-buttons: closed. Search is now the one filled button. The hero button is gone and an underlined text link "See boats and dates" replaces it.
- copy-buries-direct-booking: open. The direct-booking point is now in the headline and "for a week" is gone. But the page still shows no price or other boatyard fact to back "no fee on top of the hire".
- wide-screen-gap: closed. On widescreen, the text ends at x 1048 and the form starts at x 1133, so they read as one group. The dead band above the routes is gone on desktop and widescreen: the routes start about 50 px under the link.
- no-picture-of-the-holiday: open. The page still has no photo of a boat or a route.
- low-contrast-gray-text: closed. The route details measure 5.32:1 and the h1 measures 12.75:1 at all viewports.
- pale-form-field-borders: closed (judged by eye). The field borders are now a mid gray-green that clearly outlines each field on white, and they look 3:1 or more.
- tablet-short-intro-lines: closed. On the tablet, p.lead has 62 characters per line, and its last line is "days, and book it here.", not one word.
- phone-route-number-unit-break: closed. Each route detail on the phone stays on one line, for example "4 nights, 12 locks".
- date-field-looks-like-free-text: open. The start date is still a plain field that holds "Sat 14 June", with no date-picker cue.

**New problems.** None. No changed element is a template tell. I checked the serif h1 at weight 400, the filled Search button, the underlined text link, and the darker borders. The page uses five type sizes (40, 24, 20, 16, 14).

**What would move it most**
1. The no-fee claim has no number behind it (copy-buries-direct-booking, the remaining part). Location: the intro under the headline. The visitor reads "no fee on top of the hire" but sees no price to judge it against, so they must take it on trust. The fix: show a fact that proves the claim, such as a from-price per week for a boat at this base, near the intro or the form. The boatyard must supply the figure. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
2. A holiday page with no picture of the holiday (no-picture-of-the-holiday). Location: the hero. People hire a narrowboat for the boat and the water, and the page shows neither, so the page sells a form instead of a trip. The fix: add a real photo of the boatyard's own boats or a stretch of one of the listed routes, not a stock picture. The boatyard must supply the photo. Taste. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Start-date field: it still looks like free text. Give it a date-input or calendar cue so the visitor knows to pick a date (Nielsen heuristic 5). Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
- "See boats and dates" link: it still leads to the same place as Search. On the phone it sits above the form and is the first action the visitor reaches. Give it a clearly different job, such as browsing all boats, or remove it. Viewports: phone, tablet, desktop, widescreen.
- Tablet: the content column ends at x 664, but the nav ends at x 704. Let the content take the header's full width so the right edges line up, which also shortens the very wide 554 px form fields. Viewports: tablet.

**What's working.**
- The serif headline matches the logo and now clearly leads. It gives the page a quiet, crafted voice that suits a family boatyard.
- One filled teal Search button is now the only strong color, so the booking action is impossible to miss.
- The route list is set with each name on the left and its nights and locks right-aligned. It scans quickly, and on wide screens it ends at the same height as the form card.

It moves down to the intro, and then right to the filled teal Search button, which is now the only strong color on the page. The page reads as a calm, plain booking page for a small boatyard, with the offer and the form side by side as one group. It feels honest and quiet, but it has no picture, so it gives the viewer nothing to look forward to. On the tablet and the phone, the same order stacks into one column: headline, intro, link, form, routes. On the widescreen, the same 1024 px group sits centered.

**What it's for.** It gets a visitor to search for a narrowboat and book it direct from the boatyard (from the work order's crit).

**Verdict.** The fixes helped a lot. The phone layout now reflows, the headline leads, there is one primary action, and the text and the form sit together at every width. The biggest things still in the way are two facts that only the boatyard can supply: a price to back "no fee on top of the hire", and a real photo of the boats or the water.

- no-picture-of-the-holiday: open. The page still has no photo of a boat or a route.
- low-contrast-gray-text: closed. The route details measure 5.32:1 and the h1 measures 12.75:1 at all viewports.
- pale-form-field-borders: closed (judged by eye). The field borders are now a mid gray-green that clearly outlines each field on white, and they look 3:1 or more.
- tablet-short-intro-lines: closed. On the tablet, p.lead has 62 characters per line, and its last line is "days, and book it here.", not one word.

**New problems.** None. No changed element is a template tell. I checked the serif h1 at weight 400, the filled Search button, the underlined text link, and the darker borders. The page uses five type sizes (40, 24, 20, 16, 14).

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and no element the fix added or changed is a template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but an element the fix added or changed is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the fix added or changed as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. Added means the after image has it and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background. Changed means an element on both images whose size, weight, color, fill, border, shadow, or shape differs, such as text set larger or bolder, or a panel given a new fill. An added or changed element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and an element the fix added or changed is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.

summary:
**First read.** The eye lands on the serif headline, drops to the intro, then crosses to the white "Find a boat" card and its dark green Search button. It reads as a quiet, honest booking page for a small boatyard: calm and tidy, but it is all text and form fields. On the phone and tablet the page is one column, and the form follows straight after the intro with nothing between them. On the tablet the form now runs the full width of the header.

**What it's for.** It gets a visitor to search for a narrowboat hire direct from the boatyard (taken from the work order's crit).

**Verdict.** The fixes made the page simpler. The extra link is gone, and the tablet column now lines up with the nav. But the page still asks the visitor to take "no fee on top of the hire" on trust, and it still shows no boat and no water. Both of those need material from the boatyard.

**Finding status**
- no-fee-claim-without-number: open. At all four viewports the intro still makes the no-fee claim with no price or other boatyard fact near it or near the form.
- no-picture-of-the-holiday: open. At all four viewports the hero is still only headline and intro, with no photo of a boat or a route.
- start-date-looks-like-free-text: open. At all four viewports the start-date field is still a plain box that holds "Sat 14 June", with no calendar icon or other cue to pick a date.
- see-boats-link-duplicates-search: closed. The "See boats and dates" link is gone at all four viewports. On the phone the form now comes straight after the intro, and the page is 49 px shorter (1174 px against 1223 px).
- tablet-column-narrower-than-header: closed. On the tablet the content now ends at x 704, the same as the nav (the facts give h1, the intro and the route rows a box of 64 to 704). The form fields grew from 554 px to 594 px wide, which is the opposite of the "shorter form fields" part of the target.

**New problems.** None. The only changed elements are the wider column and form card on the tablet and the removed link. Neither one is a template tell, and nothing new was added.

**What would move it most**
1. The no-fee claim has no number behind it. Where: the intro under the headline, at every viewport. The visitor reads "no fee on top of the hire" but has no price to judge it against, so the page's main selling point stays unproven. Fix: show a fact that proves the claim near the intro or the form, such as a from-price per week for a boat at this base. Only the boatyard can supply that figure. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
2. A holiday page with no picture of the holiday. Where: the hero, at every viewport. People hire a narrowboat for the boat and the water, and the page shows neither, so it sells a form instead of a trip. Fix: add a real photo of the boatyard's own boats or of a listed route, not a stock picture. The boatyard must supply it. Taste. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- The start-date field has no date-picker cue, so the visitor cannot tell it wants a picked date (Nielsen heuristic 5). Fix: use a date input or add a calendar icon to the field. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
- On the tablet the form fields are now 594 px wide, which is very long for a value like "7 nights". Fix: put Nights and Berths side by side on one row, or cap the width of the form card. Viewports: tablet.

**What's working.**
- The page now has one clear action, Search. On the phone the visitor reaches the form right after the intro, with no competing link.
- On the tablet the logo, headline, form and route list now share one left edge and one right edge with the nav, so the column reads as one block.
- The route list ("7 nights, 38 locks") gives real, useful detail in a quiet two-column layout. Keep it.

content.content:
1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69
